chapters.title: The Visit at Dawn
paragraphs: SOCRATES. Why have you come at this hour, Crito? It must be quite early.
CRITO. Yes, very.
SOCRATES. What is the exact time?
CRITO. Dawn is just breaking.
SOCRATES. I'm surprised the prison keeper let you in.
CRITO. He knows me — I come often. And I've done him a small kindness.
SOCRATES. Did you only just arrive?
CRITO. No, I've been here a while.
SOCRATES. Then why did you sit there silently instead of waking me?

CRITO. Truly, Socrates, I would not want to be in such trouble and unrest as you are. I have been watching with amazement how peacefully you sleep. That is why I did not wake you — I wanted to spare you any extra pain. I have always thought you had a happy disposition, but I have never seen anything like the calm, easy way you bear this disaster.
SOCRATES. When a man has reached my age, Crito, he should not complain at the approach of death.
CRITO. And yet other old men face similar misfortunes, and age does not stop them from complaining.
SOCRATES. True. But you still haven't told me why you came so early.
CRITO. I bring sad and painful news. Not for you, I think — but for all of us who are your friends. And saddest of all for me.
SOCRATES. What — has the ship come back from Delos? The one whose arrival means I must die?
CRITO. The ship has not actually arrived, but it will probably be here today. People who came from Sunium say they left it there. So tomorrow, Socrates, will be your last day.
SOCRATES. Very well, Crito. If that is the will of God, I am ready. But I do not think it will arrive today.
CRITO. Why do you think that?
SOCRATES. I'll tell you. I am to die the day after the ship arrives — yes?
CRITO. Yes, that is what the authorities say.
SOCRATES. But I don't think the ship will be here until tomorrow. I infer this from a vision I had last night — or rather just now, when you kindly let me sleep.
CRITO. What was the vision?
SOCRATES. A woman appeared to me, beautiful and finely dressed, who called out: 'Socrates — on the third day from now you shall arrive in fertile Phthia.' (Homer, Iliad)
CRITO. What a strange dream, Socrates!
SOCRATES. The meaning is clear enough, I think.

chapters.title: The Plea and the Argument
paragraphs: CRITO. Yes — too clear. But Socrates, I beg you once more: take my advice and escape. If you die I lose not only an irreplaceable friend, but something else: people who don't know us will believe I could have saved you if I had been willing to spend money — and that I didn't care enough. Can there be a worse disgrace than to be thought of as someone who valued money over a friend's life? The crowd will never believe I wanted you to escape and that you refused.
SOCRATES. But why should we care about the opinion of the crowd, my dear Crito? Good people — and they are the only ones worth considering — will see things as they really happened.
CRITO. But you can see, Socrates, that the crowd's opinion does matter. What's happening to you now shows that they can do great harm to anyone who has lost their good opinion.

SOCRATES. I only wish, Crito, that the crowd could do the greatest harm — because then they could also do the greatest good, which would be wonderful. But in reality they can do neither. They cannot make a man wise or foolish. Whatever they do is the result of chance.

CRITO. All right, I won't argue with you. But tell me, Socrates — are you refusing for the sake of me and your other friends? Are you afraid that if you escape, we'll get in trouble with the informers for stealing you out, and we'll lose part or all of our property — or even something worse? If that's your worry, set it aside. To save you we ought to take this risk, or even a greater one. Listen to me, please, and do as I say.
SOCRATES. Yes, Crito — that is one of my fears, but by no means the only one.

CRITO. Don't be afraid of that one. There are people willing to get you out of prison at no great cost. The informers don't ask for much — a little money satisfies them. My own resources are ample, and they are at your service. If you have scruples about spending all of mine, foreigners will lend you theirs. Simmias of Thebes has actually brought a large sum for this very purpose. Cebes and many others are ready to spend their money to help you escape. So don't hold back on our account. And don't say, as you did at the trial, that you wouldn't know what to do with yourself elsewhere. People will welcome you wherever you go — not just in Athens. I have friends in Thessaly who would honor and protect you, and no one in Thessaly would give you any trouble. And I really don't think you are justified, Socrates, in giving up your own life when you could be saved. By doing this you are doing exactly what your enemies wanted — they want you destroyed. And you're abandoning your own children. You could raise and educate them. Instead you are leaving them to fend for themselves, and they will probably end up like other orphans. No man should bring children into the world if he is not willing to see their upbringing through. You seem to be choosing the easier path, not the better and braver one — which would have been more in keeping with someone like you, who has always claimed to care about virtue. I am ashamed not only for you but for us, your friends. People will say the whole thing was due to our cowardice. The trial need not have come on at all, or could have been managed differently. And this final folly will look as if it happened through our negligence, when we should have saved you — and you could have saved yourself, since there was no real difficulty. Look at how shameful and damaging this is, both for us and for you. Make up your mind — or rather, you should already have made it up; the time for deliberation is over. There is only one thing to do, and it must be done tonight. If we delay any longer, it will become impossible. So I beg you, Socrates — do as I say.

SOCRATES. Your zeal is precious, Crito, if it is rightly directed. If it is misdirected, the greater the zeal the greater the danger. We have to consider whether I should do what you ask. I am — and have always been — the kind of man who can only be guided by reason: by whatever argument seems best on reflection. Now that this misfortune has come, I cannot abandon my own words. The principles I have always honored I still honor. Unless we can find better principles right now, I will not agree with you — not even if the crowd's power could threaten us with more imprisonments, confiscations, and deaths. They try to scare us like children with bogeymen. So how shall we approach the question fairly? Let me return to your old argument about people's opinions. We used to say that some opinions should be respected and others not. Were we right to say this before I was condemned? Has the argument that once seemed sound now turned out to be empty talk — childish nonsense? That is what I want to consider with your help, Crito: whether, given my situation, the argument now appears different — whether I should accept it or reject it. The argument, as I recall, held that the opinions of some people should be valued and others should not. Now Crito, you are not going to die tomorrow — at least, not by any human probability. So you are disinterested, not biased by your circumstances. Tell me then: was I right to say that some opinions, and only the opinions of certain people, should be valued, while other opinions should be ignored?
CRITO. Certainly.
SOCRATES. And the good opinions are those of the wise, while the bad opinions are those of the unwise?
CRITO. Yes.
SOCRATES. The opinions of the wise are good, and the opinions of the unwise are bad?
CRITO. Certainly.

SOCRATES. And what did we say about another case? When a man dedicates himself to gymnastic training, does he attend to the praise and blame and opinion of every man — or only of one, his physician or trainer?
CRITO. Of one only.
SOCRATES. So he should fear the censure and welcome the praise of that one person, not of the crowd?
CRITO. Clearly.
SOCRATES. He should train, eat, and drink the way that single expert advises — rather than however everyone else thinks he should?
CRITO. True.
SOCRATES. And if he ignores the opinion and approval of the one expert, and follows instead the opinion of the crowd who have no expertise — won't he suffer harm?
CRITO. Certainly he will.
SOCRATES. And what is the harm — what does it affect, in the disobedient man?
CRITO. Clearly the body — that is what is destroyed by such bad choices.

SOCRATES. Good. Now isn't the same true, Crito, of other things we don't need to list one by one? In questions of just and unjust, fair and foul, good and evil — which are exactly the questions we are now considering — should we follow the opinion of the crowd and fear them? Or the opinion of the one person who actually understands? Shouldn't we fear and respect that person more than everyone else combined? And if we abandon him, won't we destroy and damage that part of us which is improved by justice and corrupted by injustice? There is such a part of us, isn't there?
CRITO. Certainly there is, Socrates.

SOCRATES. Take a parallel case. If, following the advice of those who have no expertise, we destroy the part of us that is improved by health and ruined by disease — would life be worth having? That part is the body, isn't it?
CRITO. Yes.
SOCRATES. Could we live with a corrupted, damaged body?
CRITO. Certainly not.

SOCRATES. And will life be worth living if that higher part of us — the one improved by justice and ruined by injustice — is destroyed? Do we suppose that this part of us, whatever it is, is less important than the body?
CRITO. Certainly not.
SOCRATES. More valuable than the body?
CRITO. Far more.

SOCRATES. Then, my friend, we should not pay attention to what the crowd says about us. We should pay attention to what the one person who understands justice and injustice will say — and what the truth itself will say. So you start out wrong when you advise me to follow the crowd's opinion about justice, injustice, good, evil, honor, and dishonor. — 'But,' someone will say, 'the crowd can kill us.'
CRITO. Yes, Socrates — that's exactly what someone will say.

SOCRATES. True enough. But I find with surprise that the old argument still holds. And I want to know whether another principle holds too: that what we should value most is not life itself, but a good life.
CRITO. Yes — that also still holds.
SOCRATES. And a good life is the same as a just and honorable life — does that hold too?
CRITO. Yes.

SOCRATES. From these premises let me argue the question: should I or should I not try to escape without the consent of the Athenians? If escaping is clearly the right thing, I'll attempt it. If not, I'll refrain. The other considerations you mention — money, reputation, the duty to educate one's children — I'm afraid those are just the doctrines of the crowd, who would be as quick to bring people back from the dead, if they could, as they are to put them to death — and with as little reason. So now, since the argument has carried us this far, the only remaining question is whether escaping — or letting others help me escape, paid in money and gratitude — is right. If it isn't, then the prospect of death or any other calamity from staying must not even enter into our calculation.
CRITO. I think you are right, Socrates. So how shall we proceed?

SOCRATES. Let's think it through together. Either refute me if you can, and I'll be convinced, or stop telling me I should escape against the will of the Athenians. I value your efforts to persuade me, but I cannot be persuaded against my own better judgment. So consider my first proposition and try to answer me as best you can.
CRITO. I will.

SOCRATES. Should we say that we ought never deliberately do wrong? Or that there are some times when we should and some times when we shouldn't? Or is doing wrong always evil and dishonorable, as I just said and as we have already agreed? Are all the conclusions we reached only a few days ago to be thrown out? Have we, at our age, been seriously discussing this all our lives only to discover that we are no better than children? Or, in spite of the crowd's opinion, and in spite of consequences good or bad, shall we hold to what we said then — that injustice is always evil and a dishonor to the one who does it? Shall we say so or not?
CRITO. Yes.
SOCRATES. So we must do no wrong?
CRITO. Certainly not.
SOCRATES. Nor return injury for injury, as the crowd thinks we should — for we must injure no one at all?
CRITO. Clearly not.
SOCRATES. Now, Crito — may we do evil?
CRITO. Surely not, Socrates.
SOCRATES. And what about returning evil for evil — the morality of the crowd? Is that just or not?
CRITO. Not just.
SOCRATES. Because doing evil to another is the same as injuring him?
CRITO. Very true.

SOCRATES. Then we should not retaliate or return evil for evil to anyone — no matter what evil we have suffered from him. But Crito, I want you to consider whether you really mean what you are saying. Most people will never hold this opinion. Those who agree on this point and those who don't have no common ground; they can only despise one another when they see how widely they differ. So tell me whether you actually agree with my first principle: that neither injury, retaliation, nor warding off evil with evil is ever right. Will that be the premise of our argument? Or do you reject it? I have always thought this and still do. But if you think differently, tell me. If you still hold what we used to hold, I'll move to the next step.
CRITO. Go on — I haven't changed my mind.
SOCRATES. Then to the next point, which I'll put as a question. Should a man do what he admits is right, or should he betray what is right?
CRITO. He should do what he thinks is right.

SOCRATES. Then how does that apply? If I leave the prison against the will of the Athenians, am I wronging anyone — or rather, am I not wronging those I should least of all wrong? Am I not betraying principles we agreed are just? What do you say?
CRITO. I cannot tell, Socrates — I do not know.

chapters.title: The Laws of Athens Speak
paragraphs: SOCRATES. Then consider it this way. Imagine I am about to slip out — call it whatever you like — and the Laws and the government come and question me. They say: 'Tell us, Socrates — what are you doing? By this action, aren't you trying to overturn us, the Laws, and the whole state, as far as it is in your power? Do you imagine a state can survive in which the decisions of law have no force, but are set aside and trampled on by individuals?' What shall we answer, Crito, to this and similar arguments? Anyone — especially a skilled orator — could say a great deal in defense of the law that requires sentences to be carried out. He would argue that this law should not be set aside. Shall we reply, 'Yes, but the state has injured us and given an unjust sentence'? Suppose I say that?
CRITO. Very good, Socrates.

SOCRATES. 'And was that our agreement with you?' the Laws would answer. 'Or were you to abide by the verdict of the state?' If I expressed surprise at this, the Laws would probably add: 'Answer, Socrates — instead of staring. You're used to asking and answering questions. Tell us — what complaint do you have against us that justifies you in trying to destroy us and the state? In the first place, didn't we bring you into existence? Your father married your mother through us and conceived you. Do you have any objection to those of us who govern marriage?' I would say none. 'Or against those of us who govern the upbringing and education of children, in which you yourself were trained? Were the laws governing education not right to require your father to train you in music and gymnastic?' Right, I would say. 'Well then, since you were brought into the world, raised, and educated by us — can you deny that you are our child and servant, as your forefathers were before you? And if so, you are not on equal terms with us. You cannot think you have the right to do to us what we are doing to you. Would you have any right to strike or insult or harm your father, or your master if you had one, just because you had been struck or insulted by him? — surely you would not say so. And just because we think it right to put you to death, do you think you have the right to destroy us in return — and your country, as far as you can? Will you, professor of true virtue, claim that this is justified? Has a philosopher like you failed to see that one's country is more valuable, higher and holier, than mother or father or any ancestor? More to be respected in the eyes of gods and wise men? — to be soothed and entreated when angry, even more than a father, and either to be persuaded or, if not persuaded, to be obeyed? When she punishes us — with imprisonment or beatings — the punishment must be borne in silence. If she leads us to wounds or death in battle, we follow as is right. No one may yield, retreat, or leave his post. Whether in battle, in court, or anywhere else, a man must do what his city and country command — or change their view of what is just. And if he may not do violence to his father or mother, much less may he do violence to his country.' What answer shall we give, Crito? Are the Laws speaking truly, or not?
CRITO. I think they are.

SOCRATES. Then the Laws will say: 'Consider, Socrates, whether we are speaking truly when we say that in your present attempt you would be doing us an injury. We brought you into the world, raised and educated you, gave you and every other citizen a share in every good we had to give. We further proclaim to any Athenian that, if he doesn't like us once he has come of age and seen the ways of the city and gotten to know us, he is free to go wherever he pleases and take his goods with him. None of us Laws will forbid him or interfere. Anyone who does not like us and the city, and wants to emigrate to a colony or to another city, may go where he likes, keeping his property. But anyone who has experienced how we administer justice and govern the state, and still remains, has entered into an implicit contract that he will do as we command. He who disobeys us is, we maintain, three times wrong: first, because in disobeying us he disobeys his parents; second, because we are the authors of his education; third, because he made an agreement to obey our commands — and he neither obeys them nor convinces us they are unjust. We do not impose our commands rudely; we offer the alternative of obeying or persuading us — and he does neither. These are the kinds of charges to which you, Socrates, will be exposed if you carry out your plan — you above all other Athenians.' Suppose I ask, why me especially? They will rightly retort that I, more than anyone, have acknowledged the agreement. 'There is clear proof,' they will say, 'that we and the city have not displeased you. Of all Athenians you have been the most consistent resident. You never left, so you must have loved it. You never went outside the city — except once to the Isthmus games — or anywhere else, unless you were on military service. You never traveled like other men. You had no curiosity about other states or their laws. Your affections never extended beyond us and our state. We were your special favorites. You consented to our governance of you. Here you fathered your children, which is proof of your satisfaction. Moreover, in the course of the trial you could have proposed exile as your penalty, if you had wanted to. The state which now will not let you go would have let you go then. But you pretended you preferred death to exile, and that you were not unwilling to die. Now you have forgotten those fine sentiments and show no respect for us, the Laws — you are our destroyer. You are doing what only a wretched slave would do: running away and turning your back on the agreements you made as a citizen. First, answer this: Are we right to say that you agreed to be governed by us in deed, not just in word? Is that true or not?' How shall we answer, Crito? Must we not agree?
CRITO. We can't help it, Socrates.

SOCRATES. Then they will say: 'You, Socrates, are breaking the covenants and agreements you made with us — not in haste, not under compulsion or deception, but after seventy years to think them over. During that time you were free to leave the city if we did not suit you, or if our covenants seemed unfair. You had your choice. You could have gone to Sparta or Crete, both of which you often praise for their good government, or to some other Greek or foreign state. Instead, you of all Athenians seemed especially fond of the state — that is, of us, her Laws (for who would care about a state without laws?) — that you never set foot outside her. The lame, the blind, and the maimed were not more stationary than you. And now you run away and abandon your agreements. Don't do it, Socrates, if you take our advice. Don't make yourself ridiculous by escaping the city. Just consider — if you transgress this way, what good will you do yourself or your friends? That your friends will be exiled and lose their citizenship, or lose their property, is fairly certain. As for yourself, if you flee to a nearby city like Thebes or Megara — both well governed — you will arrive as an enemy. Their government will be against you, and every patriotic citizen will look on you as a subverter of laws. You will confirm in the judges' minds the justice of their condemnation. A corrupter of laws is very likely a corrupter of the young and naive. So will you flee from well-ordered cities and virtuous men? Is life worth having on those terms? Or will you go to them shamelessly and talk to them, Socrates? And what will you say? The same things you say here — about virtue and justice and institutions and laws being the best things among men? Would that be decent of you? Surely not. But if you go to Crito's friends in Thessaly, where there is great disorder and license, they will be charmed to hear the tale of your prison-break — embellished with ridiculous details about how you wrapped yourself in a goatskin or some other disguise, in the way of fugitives. But will no one remind you that in your old age you were not ashamed to violate the most sacred laws out of a wretched desire for a little more life? Perhaps not, if you keep them in good humor. But if they're out of humor, you will hear many degrading things. You will live — but how? As the flatterer and servant of every man, eating and drinking in Thessaly, having gone abroad in order to get a meal. And where will be your fine sentiments about justice and virtue? Suppose you say you want to live for the sake of your children — to raise and educate them. Will you take them to Thessaly and strip them of Athenian citizenship? Is that the benefit you'll give them? Or do you imagine they will be better cared for and educated here if you are still alive but absent — that your friends will look after them? Do you really think your friends will look after them if you live in Thessaly, but not if you go to the next world? If those who claim to be your friends are good for anything, surely they will. Listen, Socrates, to us who raised you. Don't put life and children first and justice afterward. Put justice first, so that you may be justified before the rulers of the world below. Neither you nor any of yours will be happier or holier or more just in this life, or happier in another, if you do what Crito asks. Now you depart innocent, a sufferer and not a doer of evil — a victim of men, not of the laws. But if you go forth — returning evil for evil, injury for injury, breaking the covenants and agreements you made with us, wronging those you ought least of all to wrong, namely yourself, your friends, your country, and us — we shall be angry with you while you live. Our brothers, the Laws of the world below, will receive you as an enemy, knowing you have done your best to destroy us. Listen to us, then, and not to Crito.' This, dear Crito, is the voice I seem to hear murmuring in my ears, like the sound of the flute in the ears of a mystic. That voice is humming in my ears, and stops me from hearing any other. I know that anything more you say will be in vain. Still — speak, if you have anything to say.
CRITO. I have nothing to say, Socrates.
SOCRATES. Then leave me, Crito, to follow the will of God, and to go wherever he leads.
